title: 15 Vegetables and Herbs That Thrive In Containers More Than Garden part 6
fullText: In our previous video, we went over 15 super productive vegetables and herbs for container gardening. Have you tried growing any of them yet? Today, I'm thrilled to introduce you to 15 new varieties that guarantee equally impressive yields. Plant just a single container and you'll be harvesting for months on end. Make sure to stick around until the very end because the final plant on our list will absolutely blow you away with its massive abundant supply. So, grab your pots and let's get planting. Kicking off our list at number 15, shiso, also known as pill. Most gardeners think they have to choose between growing something beautiful and growing something productive. Shiso refuses to make you choose. If you want a plant that brings both stunning rustic visual drama and an endless harvest to your patio, this is it. It produces massive jagged purple and green leaves that look like they belong in a botanical garden. But make no mistake, it grows with the aggression of a weed. Because its growth rate is so explosive, it will quickly become rootbound in a small pot. You must give it at least a 3 to 5gallon container. You can harvest the large outer leaves every single day for wraps, salads, and garnishes. And the plant simply pushes out more from the center. You won't have to wait long. Shiso is ready for its first harvest in just 40 to 60 days, and you can pick leaves continuously until the first winter frost. It's not just about aesthetics. Shiso is a nutritional powerhouse loaded with iron, calcium, and omega-3 fatty acids. Use those massive leaves to wrap grilled meats, slice them into fresh salads, or steep them into an antioxidant richch tea. Here is a fascinating fact. In traditional Japanese cuisine, shiso isn't just used for flavor. It contains a powerful natural preservative called perilahhide, a compound that the American Chemical Society has scientifically proven to exhibit potent antimicrobial effects against food born pathogens that acts as an antidote to food poisoning, which is exactly why it has been paired with raw seafood for centuries. But there is one critical rule to keep the harvest going. You must strictly pinch off the flower spikes the moment they appear. If you let shiso go to seed, the plant assumes its life purpose is fulfilled and will completely stop producing leaves. Keep the soil consistently moist. Give it a light dose of organic fertilizer every month. And this plant will serve you non-stop until the deep frost. Moving right along to number 14, French teragon. This is the culinary secret of high-end kitchens. Most people assume that to grow premium herbs, you need a traditional, perfectly tilled garden bed. In reality, growing French teragon in a container on a spacious balcony is actually much better than putting it in the ground. French teragon is a relentless producer, but it has one fatal weakness. It absolutely despises wet feet. Winter rot kills more teragon than pests ever could. By putting it in a 5gallon pot, you take complete control over its environment. You must mix a heavy handful of perlite or coarse sand into your potting soil before planting to guarantee rapid drainage. Once established, this herb is a cut and come again machine. You simply snip the aromatic sprigs continuously throughout the summer. Patience is minimal here. You can start lightly snipping the aromatic leaves just 6 to 8 weeks after planting, continuing your harvest all the way through late fall. This herb is rich in manganese and iron, acting as a powerful natural digestive aid. In the kitchen, it is the irreplaceable soul of classic Bernz sauce. Perfect for roasting with poultry, fish, or steeping to create incredible infused vinegars. Here is a fascinating fact validated by the Royal Horicultural Society, RHS. True French teragon cannot be grown from seed because its flowers are completely sterile. That means every single French teragon plant in the world today is a living clone propagated by root division from an ancient original plant. And here is the best part. The more you trim it, the bushier and more productive it gets. Even better, every 2 years, you can simply pull it out of the container, take a sharp knife, split the root ball exactly in half, and you suddenly have double the plants. Sliding into the number 13 spot is a hidden treasure. Peanuts. Most people think peanuts belong strictly in massive open agricultural fields. They assume you need acres of loose dirt to get a meaningful harvest. That is completely false. A spacious balcony or a backyard patio is the perfect place to grow them, provided you understand how the plant actually works. Peanuts do not grow on roots. They grow from pegs that drop down from the yellow flowers, reach the soil, and bury themselves into the earth to form the nut. Therefore, you do not need a deep pot. You need a wide one. A wide, shallow tub or a 15-in diameter planter is ideal. The soil must be incredibly loose, sandy, and light so the delicate pegs can penetrate easily. Do not use heavy compacted compost. Keep the soil slightly moist, but never soggy. You plant them, you wait, you water, and at the end of the season, you get the immense, deeply satisfying experience of pulling up the entire green plant to reveal a massive hidden harvest of fresh peanuts right on your patio. Unlike continuous harvest herbs, peanuts demand a long game. They require 100 to 130 frost-free days to mature, and you'll know exactly when to pull the ultimate harvest when the green leaves begin to turn yellow and wither in early autumn. Beneath that soil lies a superfood packed with dense plant protein, healthy fats, biotin, and vitamin E. You can boil them fresh for a savory snack, roast them with sea salt, or grind them into the freshest, richest peanut butter you will ever taste. Bet you didn't know this. The peanut isn't actually a nut at all. It is a legume with a brilliant survival mechanism known in botany as geocarpy, a process heavily documented by the Botanical Society of America. The plant literally buries its own fertilized flowers underground to hide its developing offspring from hungry herbivores. At number 12, we have borage. If you want a container that becomes the vibrant, beating heart of your backyard ecosystem, you must plant borage. Most container crops focus only on leaves or roots. Borage is an unstoppable flowering machine. It pushes out hundreds of star-shaped, bright blue, edible flowers that taste surprisingly exactly like fresh cucumber. However, borage grows a very long, aggressive taproot. You cannot cram it into a small decorative pot on a window sill. It needs a deep 5gallon container to truly thrive. While it is incredibly drought tolerant and tough, to get that relentless continuous bloom, you need to water it deeply whenever the top 2 in of soil dry out. Harvest the young leaves and fresh flowers daily for salads and summer drinks. The wait is incredibly short. You can start plucking the cucumber flavored leaves in just four weeks with that endless explosion of blue flowers following right behind at week eight. These brilliant flowers are packed with vitamin C and GLA, a rare fatty acid that dramatically reduces inflammation in the body. In fact, clinical profiles from the Mount Sinai Health System verify that GLA is scientifically proven to alleviate joint pain and severe systemic inflammation. Freeze the star-shaped flowers into ice cubes to elevate your summer cocktails, or toss the young leaves into salads for a refreshing, cooling crunch. Here is a fascinating historical fact. Ancient Roman gladiators and Celtic warriors used to steep borage flowers in their wine before going into battle, firmly believing the plant bestowed absolute courage and banished all fear. But the real magic of borage is what it does for the rest of your balcony. It will draw every bee, butterfly, and pollinator in the neighborhood straight to your containers, skyrocketing the production of every other plant around it. At number 11, we have Go Cola. Sometimes the most productive plants aren't the tallest ones. They're the ones that refuse to stop spreading. Got Cola is a creeping medicinal powerhouse that thrives in the exact environments that would easily drown other herbs. It naturally grows in humid, swampy conditions across Asia, making it the perfect candidate for a container where you have absolute control over the water. Instead of a deep pot, use a wide, shallow bowl. Use a dense potting mix that holds moisture and never, ever let it dry out. You can even place a saucer of water directly under the pot to keep the roots constantly saturated. Keep it in the dappled shade of your larger patio plants. It hates the scorching afternoon sun. As it creeps over the edges of the pot, simply take a pair of scissors and give it a haircut. It will rapidly push out a fresh, dense carpet of new, highly nutritious leaves in a matter of days. This creeper wastes absolutely no time. From a healthy transplant, you can begin harvesting your first medicinal leaves in just three to four weeks, and it will produce year round if protected from the cold. This plant is legendary in natural medicine. Heavily studied for its high concentration of trurpoids, which boost brain function, improve memory, and stimulate collagen production. According to pharmarmacological reviews by the Alzheimer's Drug Discovery Foundation, these highly active triurpoids, specifically aoticide, act as powerful neurop protectors in clinical trials. Blend the fresh leaves into your morning green smoothies, juice them, or steep them into a brain boosting herbal tea. Here is a fascinating fact. In Sri Lankan folklore, ancient healers discovered this plant's brain boosting power by observing wild elephants, animals famous for their flawless memories and incredibly long lifespans, constantly seeking out and eating goa in the jungle. And just like that, we're a third of the way through our list. Which vegetable has impressed you the most so far? Let me know your thoughts down in the comments. All right, let's keep going. Breaking into the top 10 is the plant that thrives on absolute neglect. Number 10, ntorium. This is the beautiful overflowing cascade of the container garden. Both the lily pad-like leaves and the brilliant jewel toned flowers are entirely edible, offering a bold peppery kick that chefs love. This plant delivers almost instant gratification. Both the spicy leaves and the brilliant flowers are ready to be harvested in a mere 30 to 40 days and will keep blooming aggressively right up until the frost kills them. Every part of this plant is a defender of your immune system, packed with high levels of vitamin C and luteine for eye health. Use the leaves as a spicy substitute for arugula. Garnish dishes with the flowers or pickle the green seed pods into a fiery poor man's caper. A fact you probably didn't know. During World War II, when black pepper was heavily rationed and nearly impossible to find, people ingeniously dried and ground the seeds of the ntorium plant as a spicy, flawless substitute. Ntoriums are famous for trailing beautifully down the sides of large pots or hanging baskets. But many beginners make a catastrophic mistake when growing them. They treat netoriums like tomatoes. They feed them. Here is the most important rule for massive production. A technique directly backed by the agricultural experts at the Cornell University Cooperative Extension. Do not fertilize netoriums. If you give this plant rich compost or high nitrogen fertilizer, it will produce a massive, lush jungle of green leaves and absolutely zero flowers. Plant them in poor, cheap potting soil. Put them in a 3gon pot and let the soil dry out slightly between waterings. The ntorium operates on a very specific survival mechanism. The harder the soil, the poorer the nutrients, the more aggressively it blooms. Treat it poorly and it will reward you with months of endless flowers. Down at number nine, we have horseradish. This is not a delicate herb. This is the beast in the pot. In a traditional backyard garden, planting horseradish is often a nightmare. It spreads relentlessly underground and takes over entire garden beds, becoming almost impossible to eradicate. That is exactly why you must grow it in a container. But you cannot use a normal pot. You need a massive one. A 10 to 15 gallon half barrel is perfect. Horseradish needs deep, loose soil to push its thick, spicy taproots downward without hitting a wall. It is a heavy drinker, so you must keep the soil consistently damp during the peak heat of summer. It will grow massive, dramatic green leaves all season. Then, when winter approaches and the leaves die back, tip the barrel over. Snap off the largest, thickest roots for your kitchen. While you can sparingly snip the green leaves during the summer, the true root harvest requires patience. The massive taproots need 140 to 160 days underground and are best dug up in late autumn, right after the very first frost concentrates their fiery flavor. That intense spice comes from glucosinylates, powerful biological compounds that clear your sinuses instantly and kickstart your immune system. Grate the fresh, pungent root directly over roasted meats. Blend it into a fiery cocktail or use it to make a devastatingly fresh, authentic wasabi substitute. Here is a fascinating fact. An intact horseradish root has absolutely no smell or spice. According to the journal of agricultural and food chemistry, the legendary heat is only created through a violent chemical reaction between glucosinylates and an enzyme called myroinase that occurs the exact moment the plant cells are crushed and exposed to oxygen. And the real magic, simply take a 2-in piece of the remaining root, drop it back into the soil, and it will regrow the following spring without fail. It is a permanent indestructible food source. Number eight, water spinach or Kong Kong. Every container gardener knows the midsummer struggle. The brutal heat arrives, the lettuce melts, the kale wilts, and the garden stops producing. That is precisely when water spinach is just waking up. This semi-aquatic plant is the absolute undisputed champion of hot, humid weather. Because it naturally grows in swamps and slow-moving rivers, you have to break the ultimate cardinal rule of container gardening. You do not need drainage. In fact, a large sealed plastic tub filled with heavy potting mix and water, essentially creating pure mud, is exactly what this plant wants. It is a voracious, unstoppable feeder. Give it a liquid nitrogen fertilizer every 2 weeks and the hollow vines will literally explode with growth. You can cut the thick stems down to just a few inches above the soil line and within days they will shoot right back up. You can harvest heavy baskets of fresh greens every single week until the weather turns cold. Speed is its absolute superpower. You can make your very first massive cut just 3 to 4 weeks after planting, and the vines recover so violently fast that you can repeat that heavy harvest every 10 to 14 days. These hollow vines are an absolute gold mine of iron, calcium, and vitamin A. In the kitchen, it is the undisputed king of Asian stir fries. Flash fry the stems with crushed garlic and oyster sauce for a legendary nutrient-dense side dish that retains an incredible crunch. A fact you probably didn't know. Water spinach grows so violently fast, up to 4 in in a single day under ideal conditions, that the USDA Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, Aphus, actually heavily regulates it as an invasive, noxious weed in several states because it can completely choke out wild rivers. At number seven, we have lovage. Imagine the sharp savory flavor of celery but amplified. Growing on a plant that simply refuses to quit. Lovage is a towering architectural giant of an herb. It can easily reach 5 to 6 ft tall, making it a stunning visual centerpiece for a spacious balcony. Because of its massive size and incredibly deep roots, a flimsy plastic pot will not work. You need a heavy 10 to 15gallon container. So a strong gust of wind doesn't blow the entire plant over. Lovage loves rich, lomy soil, so you must mix in plenty of compost before planting. It is also incredibly cold hearty, often surviving harsh winters right in the pot. The best part, you only need one single plant. You snip the strong hollow stems and leaves continuously for soups, broths, and stews. You can start snipping the outer stalks of a young transplant in just 4 to 6 weeks. From that moment on, it is a relentless producer from early spring all the way to the late autumn frost. Love is loaded with B vitamins and queretin, acting as a powerful natural diuretic to flush toxins from your body. Because the flavor is so intense, a single hollow stem can transform a bland potato soup or a hearty winter stew into a culinary masterpiece. Here is a fascinating fact documented in the historical archives of the Herb Society of America. The hollow stems of lovage are so sturdy and flavorful that ancient Roman travelers would cut them and use them as natural edible drinking straws to infuse their water and wine on long journeys. Every time you cut it back, it responds by pushing out lush, tender new growth from the base. It is the ultimate cut and come again perennial. Coming in at number six, taro, also known as collocasia. If you have a spacious backyard patio and you want to turn it into a high calorie food forest, this is your plant. Taro produces massive dramatic elephant ear leaves that instantly give your garden a lush tropical jungle vibe. But while the leaves look beautiful above ground, below the soil the plant is silently producing a dense starchy harvest. Taro loves water. It demands massive containers. Think a 15 or 20 gallon tub. In fact, to keep it happy, you can place the heavy pot inside a larger saucer constantly filled with water to ensure the roots never dry out. It is an incredibly heavy feeder. You must mix in a slowrelease organic fertilizer at planting and top dress with thick compost mid-season. The beauty of container tarot is its dual harvest. You can continuously harvest the young unfurling outer stalks for cooking throughout the entire summer while the massive tubers continue to swell beneath the soil for a massive autumn harvest. This plant operates on a brilliant dual timeline. You can start harvesting the young outer stalks continuously after just 8 weeks while the survival tubers quietly swell underground requiring a full 7 to 8 months before the grand late autumn harvest. This produces a vital survival crop. dense tubers packed with complex carbohydrates, dietary fiber, vitamin E, and potassium. But a critical warning, tarot leaves and tubers contain calcium oxalate crystals and must be cooked thoroughly before eating. Once boiled or roasted, the tubers become a creamy, nutty staple, while the massive leaves can be steamed to wrap savory meat. Here is a fascinating fact. Taro is widely considered by archaeologists to be one of the oldest cultivated crops in human history. According to UNESCO archaeological data from the Cook Swamp site in Papua New Guinea, researchers found definitive evidence that it has been successfully grown and consumed for over 10,000 years and famously used to fuel ancient Polynesian voyagers across the Pacific Ocean. Not only is it a stunning flower for decorating the garden, but it also provides a fantastic, nutritious harvest. Do you agree with me? Let me know down in the comments. Now, let's move on to the top five on today's list. Make sure to stick around until the very end because the final plant is going to completely surprise you. At number five, we have Oka, the New Zealand yam. This is the autumn surprise of the container garden. While most vegetables are dying back and giving up as the days get shorter, oka is just getting ready to perform. The plant itself is gorgeous, forming a dense bush of clover-like leaves and bright red stems. But the real prize lies underground. Incredibly crisp, tangy, neon colored tubers. Okcha only begins to form these underground tubers when the daylight hours drop significantly in late autumn, meaning it needs a very long growing season. A 7 to 10 gallon heavyduty grow bag is perfect. The secret to a massive overflowing harvest is a technique called hilling. Just like potatoes, as the ocha plant grows taller, you must continuously add more soil to the container, burying the lower stems. Keep the soil moist but well drained. Protect the leaves from the very first light frosts, and you will dump out a literal mountain of vibrant jewelike tubers in early winter. Patience is mandatory for this autumn surprise. Okcha requires a long 6 to 8month growing season, and you absolutely cannot harvest until the daylight hours drop significantly in late autumn or early winter, which is the exact trigger for the tubers to form. Okcha is a nutritional anomaly, a low calorie carbohydrate loaded with vitamin C, potassium, and iron. Unlike potatoes, you don't even have to cook okra. Slice the vibrant tubers raw into salads for a lemony apple-like crunch, or roast them whole until they become sweet and savory. A fact you probably didn't know. In its native Andes Mountains, indigenous farmers have a brilliant trick, which was thoroughly documented in the botanical report, Lost Crops of the Incas, by the National Research Council. After harvesting, they leave the Okcha tubers out in the freezing high altitude sunlight for a few days, which magically converts the plant's natural organic acids into pure sweet sugar. Number four, Yakon, the Bolivian sunroot. Prepare to be absolutely shocked by how much food a single pot can produce. Yakon is a towering giant that yields massive, sweet, crunchy tubers that taste like a refreshing cross between an apple and a watermelon. Because this plant will easily reach 5 to 6 feet tall with massive velvet-like leaves, a standard pot is useless. You need a massive 15 to 20 gallon container or a heavyduty fabric grow bag. It requires incredibly rich, lomy soil and a tremendous amount of water. During the blazing summer months, those massive leaves will transpire water at an astonishing rate. So, daily deep watering is absolutely non-negotiable. If it dries out, the yield plummet, but if you keep it fed and watered, the payoff is staggering. At the end of the season, when the top finally dies back from the frost, one single pot can easily yield 10 to 20 pounds of sweet, juicy roots. This giant plays the long game. It needs a full 6 to 7 months of growth. And the golden rule is to wait until the first heavy frost completely kills the top velvet leaves. That is your exact signal to dig up the massive winter harvest. Yakone is a literal miracle for your metabolism. The massive crunchy tubers are packed with inulin, a prebiotic fiber that tastes sweet but has a near zero glycemic index, meaning it won't spike your blood sugar, a mechanism scientifically validated by clinical studies from the National Institutes of Health. Slice the juicy roots raw into fruit salads, juice them for a naturally sweet drink, or roast them for a diet friendly dessert. A fact you probably didn't know. The ancient Incas called Yakone the water route. Because the tubers are up to 90% water, indigenous messengers running across the arid Andes mountains would dig them up purely to quench their thirst. At number three, we have stevia. Why buy chemically processed sweeteners when you can grow a continuous natural sugar factory right on your balcony? Stevia leaves are incredibly sweet and the plant actually thrives in container life. A 3 to 5gallon pot is perfectly sufficient for a massive harvest. But stevia requires a delicate watering balance. It hates drying out and wilts quickly, but its roots will rapidly rot in completely soggy soil. You must use a premium well- draining potting mix and water it only when the top inch of soil feels dry to the touch. To get a relentless, continuous harvest, you must be ruthless. You must continuously pinch off the growing tips. This stops the plant from getting tall, spindly, and flowering, forcing it to branch out into a dense, highly productive shrub. Snip the leaves, dry them, crush them, and you have an endless supply of natural sweetness all season long. Your natural sugar factory is operational almost immediately. You can start picking sweet leaves in 40 to 60 days, though the absolute peak sweetness occurs in late summer, right before the plant attempts to flower. The leaves contain stevialol glycosides, compounds up to 300 times sweeter than sugar, but with absolutely zero calories and zero impact on your blood sugar. The European Food Safety Authority, EFSA, confirms that because the human body lacks the enzymes to break down these molecules, they pass through completely unabsorbed. You can use this fine powder as an endless natural way to sweeten your coffee, tea. Here is a fascinating fact. Long before it became a modern diet trend, the Guadi people of South America used stevia for over 1,500 years, calling it sweet herb and using it specifically to balance the bitter taste of their traditional medicinal teas. This sprawling vining plant is a medicinal powerhouse that seems completely and totally immune to pests, diseases, and harsh conditions. In a spacious balcony setting, you can plant it in a 5gallon hanging basket and let it cascade beautifully, or give it a tall trellis to climb. It prefers bright indirect light rather than scorching full afternoon sun. It earned its name for a reason. Scientifically proven to lower blood sugar, reduce cholesterol, and fight inflammation. A comprehensive pharmarmacological review published in the journal Frontiers in Pharmarmacology specifically confirms that its leaves possess potent antid-diabetic and anti-hypertensive properties that actively mimic insulin. You can toss these leaves raw into fresh salads, blend them into detox green smoothies, or flash fry them with crushed garlic for a nutrient-dense side dish. Here is a fascinating fact. For centuries, the exact location and cultivation methods of longevity spinach were closely guarded secrets among traditional herbalists in Asia. considered too valuable of a life- extending medicine to share with the general public. The magic of longevity spinach is its recovery speed. The more you harvest the crisp, slightly fleshy leaves, the more aggressively it branches out to replace them. And if you ever want more plants, it is ridiculously easy to propagate. Simply snap off a stem, strip the bottom leaves, and stick it directly into damp potting soil. It roots almost instantly. From a simple cutting to your first harvest takes an astonishingly short 3 to four weeks. After that, it is a daily harvest machine that will produce 365 days a year if you protect it from winter temperatures. You can harvest from this plant every single day, and it will never ever show signs of stopping. And finally, taking the absolute crown at number one, Cuban oregano, also known as Mexican mint. If there is one plant that could survive the end of the world in a plastic pot, this is it. Cuban oregano is not a true oregano. It is a stunning semisucculent with thick, velvety, incredibly aromatic leaves that carry the intense, punchy flavor of oregano, thyme, and mint all rolled into one. This plant is practically indestructible. It demands a container. A 3 to 5gallon pot is ideal because it absolutely requires sandy cactus-like soil with supreme drainage. It laughs at heat waves. It thrives on utter neglect. You can go on vacation, forget to water it for a week in the blazing sun, and its thick leaves will simply hold the moisture it needs to survive. The velvet leaves are loaded with vitamins's A and C and have been used for centuries as a traditional medicinal remedy to cure sore throats and chest coughs. Crush the thick leaves into intense sauces. Use them as a dominant marinade for pork and poultry or steep them into a powerful medicinal tea. 99% of people don't know this fact. Despite its famous name, Cuban oregano is entirely a lie. As officially verified by the botist at the Royal Botanic Gardens Q, it is not an oregano and it does not originate from Cuba. It is actually a highly evolved member of the mint family. Originally hailing from the rugged terrains of southern Africa, to harvest, you don't even need scissors. Just snap off the fleshy branches with your fingers. The plant immediately heals the wound and shoots out two new branches in its place. Once established from a cutting, it is ready to harvest in as little as 4 weeks. Because it is an evergreen perennial in warm climates, it ignores the seasons completely, giving you a relentless harvest every single month of the year. It is the undisputed king of the continuous harvest. A flawless, beautiful, unstoppable food source that will transform your balcony into an endless supply of flavor.
